what_it_does: Running a large language model (LLM) efficiently requires shrinking the numbers used to represent the model's billions of parameters — a process called quantization, where high-precision floating-point numbers are replaced with smaller, lower-precision ones that take less memory and compute faster. One proposed standard for this is called Microscaling (MX) format, a way of grouping numbers and sharing a common scale factor so that each individual value can be stored with fewer bits without losing too much accuracy; however, practical hardware that can actually execute MX-format arithmetic has been lacking. This paper presents a joint algorithm-and-hardware design: on the algorithm side, a revised version of MX format (called RMX) is introduced with a new strategy for choosing which direction to group numbers, improving how faithfully the compressed values represent the originals. On the hardware side, a matching accelerator chip design (RMFA) is built around this revised format, with arithmetic units and data-encoding circuits tuned specifically for low-bit RMX operations. The goal is to make MX-style quantization practically deployable for LLM inference, rather than just theoretically attractive.
